reason: Tells the learner to classify by the property lost, not the mechanism, and warns that the same technology (encryption) can be a control or a weapon. That fixes the ransomware trap where 'encrypts' pulls people toward Confidentiality.

Gives a concrete three-way test (sees / changes / can't use) plus a tie-break by primary goal over side effects. It goes past hint 0 by handling items with mixed damage, such as exfiltrate-and-post or tampered firmware.

Separates the two identity buckets on timing and purpose: gatekeeping before an action versus evidence left after it. That correctly puts the signed payment and the tamper-evident log under Non-repudiation, and the MFA and fingerprint under Authentication.

Adds a different axis that hint 0 lacks: the organisation's interest versus the individual's control. This is what pulls data minimisation and erasure into Privacy, so it complements hint 0 without repeating it.

Gives a usable 'what does the enforcing' classifier (machine / people following a rule / physical barrier) that maps directly onto the three buckets. Disk encryption goes to Technical and the fence and door go to Physical.

The counterfactual 'would it keep working if people stopped following instructions' test, together with 'paperwork or not', targets the background-check case. Learners often miss that a process with no document is still Administrative. It only splits Administrative from the rest, but that is the hard boundary, and hint 0 does not cover it.

The 'would you owe this even if nobody had hired you' test cleanly isolates Canon III (conflict of interest, declining work you are not qualified for). It then sends the rest to public harm, own conduct or the field, and it handles the sales-pitch prospect correctly, since a prospect is not a principal, so that item goes to II.

Warns that honesty runs through almost every item and does not discriminate, which matters for 'tell the client up front' (honest, but it belongs to the engagement, so III). It does partly re-list hint 0's four relationships, so the overlap is noticeable, but the warning itself is new.
Gives a real method (order by input dependencies, not by importance). It is close to generic and would apply to any ordering task, but it does settle identify, then assess, then choose.

Targets the one non-obvious adjacency: residual-risk sign-off comes after the control is applied and verified, because acceptance has to rest on what the control actually achieved. That adds something specific hint 0 does not.

Gives a three-axis classifier: binding vs advised (Guideline); goal, named setting or sequence of actions (Policy, Standard, Procedure); and internal vs external (Law). That resolves nearly every item, including 'named owner' as Policy.

This mostly restates hint 0's point that bindingness and specificity are separate questions, and 'naming what to use is not how to do it' is already in hint 0's setting-versus-series-of-actions split. A learner still stuck after hint 0 gets little new. A replacement could, for example, flag hedge words ('where practical', 'prefer') as the Guideline signal, or point to who issued the item as the Law signal.
